extracted.intended_audience: practitioners and respondents in USPTO trademark disciplinary proceedings; trademark attorneys; USPTO Office of Enrollment and Discipline (OED) participants
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and rules applied by the USPTO/OED and courts to evaluate alleged misconduct in trademark matters, including who may practice, signature and filing requirements, deceit/misrepresentation rules, competence, aiding unauthorized practice, and burdens for defenses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Who may practice in trademark matters (37 C.F.R. § 11.14)
rubrics_metrics.description: Only the individuals identified in § 11.14 may practice before the Office in trademark matters: (a) attorneys; (b) non-lawyers recognized to practice before the Office in trademark matters prior to January 1, 1957; and (c) foreign attorneys specially recognized by the USPTO for the limited purpose of representing parties located in their country.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only the aforementioned individuals are permitted to practice before the Office in trademark matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition/scope of practice before the Office (37 C.F.R. § 11.5(b)(2))
rubrics_metrics.description: Practice before the Office in trademark matters includes, but is not limited to, consulting with or giving advice to a client in contemplation of filing a trademark application or other document with the Office; preparing and prosecuting an application for trademark registration; preparing an amendment that may require written argument to establish registrability; conducting opposition, cancellation, or concurrent use proceedings; and conducting an appeal to the Trademark Trial and Appeal Board.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An individual who is not authorized to practice in trademark matters may not sign documents on behalf of applicants; they may, however, act as a domestic representative or correspondent (limited to receiving correspondence and process).

rubrics_metrics.name: Domestic representative/correspondent role and limits (TMEP § 608.01)
rubrics_metrics.description: A domestic representative is an individual who serves and receives correspondence and process on behalf of an overseas client. Such an individual may act as a domestic representative or correspondent but may not sign documents on behalf of applicants unless authorized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Merely forwarding correspondence is allowed, but preparing, completing, electronically signing, or submitting trademark applications or substantive responses constitutes practice before the Office and exceeds the domestic representative role.

rubrics_metrics.name: Signature requirements for trademark documents
rubrics_metrics.description: Signatories must personally sign trademark documents; electronically affixing another person's signature without indicating otherwise is misleading and improper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Affixing clients' electronic signatures, completing documents by entering applicants' electronic signatures, or signing Change of Correspondence forms when not the applicant, a person with legal authority to bind the applicant, or a qualified practitioner violates the Rules of Practice and may constitute deceit or forgery. TEAS signature options should be understood and used correctly (e.g., HSign-on).

rubrics_metrics.name: Disreputable conduct (37 C.F.R. § 10.23(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Disreputable conduct' includes unprofessional conduct violative of ordinary standards of professional obligation and honor; misconduct need not be enumerated in the disciplinary rules to be disreputable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Violations of the Rules of Practice (e.g., unauthorized filing, forged signatures) that do not comply with USPTO practices may be considered disreputable. Case law shows a wide range of conduct (including criminal convictions) can fall within this standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on deceit, fraud, or misrepresentation (37 C.F.R. § 10.23(b)(4); § 11.804(c))
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners shall not engage in conduct involving dishonesty, fraud, deceit, or misrepresentation. Misrepresentation includes false or misleading assertions by words or conduct; concealment or non-disclosure may also amount to misrepresentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Forgery of signatures, signing documents without indicating the signature was made by someone other than the purported signatory, or filing documents that mislead USPTO examiners about who actually signed are examples of deceit. Case citations: Iowa Supreme Ct. Attorney Disciplinary Bd. v. Liles; Disciplinary Counsel v. Wilson; In re Lane; In re Uchendu.

rubrics_metrics.name: Failure to correct misrepresentations to the Office (37 C.F.R. § 11.303(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners shall not knowingly make a false statement of fact or law to a tribunal or fail to correct a false statement of material fact or law previously made to the tribunal by the practitioner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 'Knowingly' means actual knowledge or knowledge inferred from circumstances; intent to deceive is not required. Failure to correct prior false representations (even absent intent) violates ethical rules. See In re Fuller and related authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Competence requirement (37 C.F.R. § 10.77(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners must not handle a legal matter that they know or should know they are not competent to handle without associating with a practitioner who is competent to handle it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Competence includes knowing applicable rules and procedures (e.g., TEAS signature requirements, Rules of Practice, TMEP). A practitioner who agrees to represent clients must inform themselves of the applicable rules or associate counsel; failure to do so (and then forging or misusing signatures) violates the competence rule. Case citations: Reibman v. Senie; Attorney Grievance Comm'n of Maryland v. Zhang.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on aiding unauthorized practice of law (37 C.F.R. § 11.505)
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners may not practice law in a jurisdiction in violation of that jurisdiction's rules or assist another in doing so.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determination requires a two-step analysis: (1) determine whether actions by the third party constitute unauthorized practice before the Office; (2) determine whether the respondent aided those actions. Preparation of legal documents generally constitutes the practice of law, though merely filing or receiving correspondence (or attaching a handwritten signature PDF) may not. Cases: Geauga Cty. Bar Ass'n v. Haig; Real Estate Bar Ass'n v. Nat'l Real Estate Info. Servs.; In re Peel; Drew v. Unauthorized Practice of Law Comm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between unauthorized practice and non-legal ministerial acts
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain ministerial acts (e.g., merely filing Statements of Use with attached PDFs of applicants' handwritten signatures; receiving and filing correspondence; completing forms that have no legal implications) may not by themselves constitute the unauthorized practice of law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts distinguish between drafting/performing legal work (practice of law) and mere signature/filing tasks. Even improper signing of such ministerial forms may be wrong, but not necessarily rise to unauthorized practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conduct prejudicial to the administration of justice (37 C.F.R. § 10.23(b)(5); § 11.804(d))
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioner conduct is prejudicial to the administration of justice when it negatively impacts the public's perception or efficacy of the courts or legal profession, or interferes with efficient operation of the court/Office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unauthorized practice before the Office, filing documents with forged signatures, and knowingly defying exclusion orders are examples that have been found prejudicial. Case citations: United States v. Johnson; In re Vohra; Iowa Supreme Ct. Attorney Disciplinary Bd. v. Liles; In re Kroll.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on false or misleading communications about services (37 C.F.R. § 11.701)
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners shall not make false or misleading communications about themselves or their services.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In disciplinary proceedings, the OED must prove false/misleading communications by clear and convincing evidence; mere representation that one can act as a domestic representative is not the same as representing authorization to practice, and lack of evidence will defeat this charge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Catch-all: conduct adversely reflecting on fitness to practice (37 C.F.R. § 10.23(b)(6))
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners shall not 'engage in any other conduct that adversely reflects on the practitioner's fitness to practice before the Office.' This subsection is a catch-all for conduct not covered by other subsections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If alleged conduct violates any provision of § 10.23(b)(1) through (b)(5), it cannot also be separately charged under (b)(6).

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden and form for asserting affirmative defenses (37 C.F.R. §§ 11.49, 11.36(c))
rubrics_metrics.description: In a disciplinary proceeding, the respondent has the burden of proving any affirmative defense by clear and convincing evidence. Such defenses must be stated affirmatively in the Answer and must draw a nexus between the defense and the misconduct and explain why it provides defense or mitigation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Generally, a respondent may not rely on a defense not raised in the Answer, although the Court may allow a late filing for good cause.

rubrics_metrics.name: Due process standards in disciplinary proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: The Due Process Clause requires that an individual be given an opportunity to be heard before being deprived of a significant property interest; this includes notice of allegations and a meaningful opportunity to present a defense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Amended Complaint's recitation of facts and alleged disciplinary rules can satisfy notice; active participation in a hearing and understanding of the allegations weighs against a successful due-process claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard for selective enforcement/ selective prosecution claims
rubrics_metrics.description: To prevail on a selective enforcement claim, a respondent must demonstrate (1) she has been singled out while other similarly situated violators were left untouched; and (2) the prosecutorial decision was made invidiously or in bad faith (e.g., based on race, religion, or to prevent exercise of constitutional rights).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A presumption of regularity supports prosecutorial decisions; mere evidence of selectivity without proof of improper purpose is insufficient. Case citations: United States v. Armstrong; United States v. Hendrickson.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and scope of 'misrepresentation' (case law guidance)
rubrics_metrics.description: A misrepresentation is the act of making a false or misleading assertion (by words or conduct), usually with intent to deceive; concealment or non-disclosure may have the effect of a misrepresentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Falsely signing a document and submitting it is a false representation even if the document's substantive content is accurate because the signature misleads. (Citing Lane; Black's Law Dictionary; In re Uchendu.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Knowledge standard for ethical violations (37 C.F.R. § 11.1; § 11.303 context)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Knowingly' means actual knowledge of the fact in question and can be inferred from circumstances; intent to deceive is not required for some violations (e.g., failure to correct false statements).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A practitioner's knowledge may be inferred from circumstances such as the nature of filings and subsequent communications, and ignorance of the rule is not a defense when the practitioner should have known the applicable rules.
